title: The Universe and Space Exploration
seo_title: Grade 9 Science (SNC1W): The Universe and Space Exploration Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: Evidence for theories of the origin and evolution of the universe and the solar system; stars and galaxies; distances in space in astronomical units and light-years; and the social, environmental and economic impacts of space exploration and the technologies that come from it, including Canadian contributions. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Science, Grade 9: SNC1W (2022), Strand E: Space Exploration)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Science (SNC1W) worksheets on the universe and space exploration: light-years, the life cycle of stars, galaxies, the big bang, satellites, the Canadarm and space technology. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and is still expanding.
body_html:
How to think about it

Distances in space are huge. The astronomical unit (AU) is the average distance from Earth to the Sun (about 150 million km). A light-year is the distance light travels in a year (about 9.46 × 10¹² km). Stars form from clouds of gas and dust, shine by fusion, and end as white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes depending on their mass.

Evidence for the big bang includes the red shift of distant galaxies (the universe is expanding) and the cosmic microwave background. Space technology such as satellites, GPS, weather and climate monitoring and the Canadarm brings many benefits, but also costs, risks and space debris.

Example

Light from a star takes 4 years to reach us. How far away is it?

Distance = 4 light-years

Answer: about 3.8 × 10¹³ km

Example

A galaxy's light is shifted towards red. What does this tell us?

The wavelength is stretched.

Answer: it is moving away from us

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a light-year is a unit of time.
  • Saying all stars end as black holes.
  • Thinking satellites stay up because there is no gravity in space.

faq.q: Why do we see distant galaxies as they were long ago?
faq.a: Their light took millions or billions of years to reach us.

faq.q: What are some Canadian contributions to space exploration?
faq.a: The Canadarm robotic arms, RADARSAT Earth-observation satellites, and Canadian astronauts on the space station and on the Artemis II crew.

items.q: Proxima Centauri (the nearest star after the Sun) is 4.2 light years away. How long does its light take to reach us?
items.e: One light year is the distance light travels in a year.

items.q: What does it mean that Arcturus is 37 light years away?
c: It takes 37 years to fly there by plane.
Light from it takes 37 years to reach Earth.
items.e: A light year is a distance, not a time.

items.q: What does it mean that Betelgeuse is 550 light years away?
c: Light from it takes 550 years to reach Earth.
It takes 550 years to fly there by plane.
items.e: A light year is a distance, not a time.

sets.title: The origin of the solar system and elements

items.q: In a massive star, 4 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 4 × 2 = 8 protons → oxygen.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Stromatolite fossils about 3.5 billion years old?
c: Earth had solid crust and probably liquid water very early.
Simple microbial life existed very early.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: In a massive star, 10 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 10 × 2 = 20 protons → calcium.

items.q: In a massive star, 3 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 3 × 2 = 6 protons → carbon.

items.q: In a star, 7 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 7 = 28; atomic number 2 × 7 = 14 (silicon).

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: They happened at the same time.
oxygen begins to build up in the air
items.e: The first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 8 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 8 × 2 = 16 protons → sulfur.

items.q: In a star, 5 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 5 = 20; atomic number 2 × 5 = 10 (neon).

items.q: Which evidence best supports this idea: “Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.”
c: Stromatolite fossils about 3.5 billion years old
Banded iron formations about 2.5 billion years old
Heavily cratered surfaces on the Moon and Mercury
items.e: Match the evidence to the claim.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/32 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/32 = 5 half-lives; 5 × 5730 = 28650 years.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Banded iron formations about 2.5 billion years old?
c: Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
Simple microbial life existed very early.
The early solar system had many large impacts.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/4 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/4 = 2 half-lives; 2 × 5730 = 11460 years.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: the Moon forms after a giant impact
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the first animals appear, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 7 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 7 × 2 = 14 protons → silicon.

items.q: Which happened first: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: the Moon forms after a giant impact
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Meteorites?
c: Earth had solid crust and probably liquid water very early.
Simple microbial life existed very early.
The early solar system had many large impacts.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: A rock has uranium-235 and lead-207 in a ratio of 1 : 63 (half-life of uranium-235: 704 million years). How old is it? (Assume all the lead-207 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 63 means 1/64 is left → 6 half-lives = 4224 million years.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago.

items.q: What is one environmental concern about rocket launches?
c: they release exhaust gases and particles into the atmosphere
they make the Moon move away
items.e: Launches also add to space debris if stages are left in orbit.

items.q: What is space debris?
c: old satellites, rocket stages and fragments left in orbit
clouds of gas around the Sun
items.e: Even small pieces move at about 28 000 km/h and can damage working spacecraft.

items.q: Why do astronauts need spacesuits on a spacewalk?
c: space has no air to breathe, almost no pressure, extreme temperatures and strong radiation
the suits let them breathe the gases in space
the suits stop gravity from acting
items.e: The suit is a small spacecraft with its own air, pressure, cooling and radiation shield.

items.q: How do satellites help us study climate change?
c: they make rain fall over deserts
they measure ice cover, sea level, sea-surface temperature and greenhouse gases from orbit
they cool Earth by blocking sunlight
they remove carbon dioxide from the air
items.e: Remote sensing from orbit gives regular data for the whole planet.

items.q: What is remote sensing?
c: measuring soil with a probe in the ground
listening to radio stations far away
collecting information about Earth from a distance, for example with satellite images
items.e: Satellites carry cameras and sensors that record light, heat and radar signals.

items.q: Why do some Indigenous knowledge keepers and scientists both study the night sky?
c: stars can be seen only from space
the sky only changes once a century
the sky has been used for navigation, calendars and stories for thousands of years
items.e: Many peoples used star patterns to mark seasons for hunting, fishing and planting.

items.q: How did satellites change weather forecasting?
c: they track clouds and storms over oceans and remote areas in real time
they make the weather the same everywhere
they replaced thermometers on the ground
items.e: Images every few minutes let forecasters follow storms as they develop.

items.q: Which instrument on a satellite measures heat given off by the ground and oceans?
items.e: Warm objects give off infrared radiation, so the sensor can map temperatures.

items.q: How can satellite data help farmers?
c: satellites stop insects from eating crops
satellites make the growing season longer
images show which parts of a field are dry, unhealthy or need fertilizer
items.e: This is called precision agriculture.

items.q: What is a spin-off technology?
c: a product first developed for space that is later used on Earth
a rocket that is used again
a satellite that spins to stay stable
items.e: Examples include better water filters, memory foam and scratch-resistant lenses.

items.q: What is one reason space exploration is expensive?
c: space has no gravity, so nothing can be built
fuel is free but the paint is costly
satellites can only be launched once a century
rockets, spacecraft and life-support systems must be built and tested to be extremely reliable
items.e: Agencies share costs through international projects such as the space station.

items.q: Which technology uses signals from several satellites to find your position?
items.e: A receiver times signals from at least four satellites to work out its position.

items.q: How do communication satellites help remote northern communities?
c: they relay phone, internet and television signals where there are no cables
they melt snow on the roads
items.e: Many Arctic communities depend on satellite links for internet and health services.

items.q: Which body is the next major human destination planned by NASA's Artemis program, with Canadian participation?
items.e: Canada is building Canadarm3 for the Gateway station that will orbit the Moon.

items.q: Why is space debris a growing problem?
c: it blocks all sunlight from Earth
collisions make more pieces, which can damage satellites and the space station
items.e: More launches and collisions add to the debris; agencies track larger pieces.

items.q: What did the Hubble Space Telescope help astronomers measure?
c: the expansion of the universe and the distances to galaxies
the speed of sound in air
items.e: Hubble observations of distant galaxies refined the age of the universe to about 13.8 billion years.

items.q: What powers most satellites and the space station?
items.e: Sunlight is strong and constant in orbit, and the panels charge batteries for the dark part of each orbit.

items.q: What does the Canadarm do on a space station or shuttle?
c: it measures the temperature of the Sun
it is a robotic arm that moves equipment, catches spacecraft and helps astronauts
it makes oxygen for the crew
items.e: The Canadarm, Canadarm2 and Dextre are Canadian robotic systems used in space.

items.q: Which kind of orbit keeps a satellite above the same spot on the equator?
items.e: At about 36 000 km up, the satellite circles once a day, matching Earth's rotation.

items.q: What can RADARSAT satellites see that ordinary cameras cannot?
c: the ground through clouds and darkness, using radar
items.e: Radar sends out microwaves and records the echoes, so it works day and night.
